section.title: The Fall of Babylon
section.sectionRationale: Chapter 18 completes the Babylon sequence begun in chapter 17, moving from interpretation to a full funeral dirge over the great city's sudden fall, sung in turn by an angel, a heavenly voice, the kings of the earth, the merchants, and the sailors of the world, before heaven itself is called to rejoice. It is bounded by the descending angel's cry that Babylon the great has fallen and the mighty angel's symbolic millstone at the chapter's close, and it stands in deliberate, stark contrast to the marriage of the Lamb announced immediately afterward in chapter 19.
section.thesis: Babylon the great, drunk on luxury and complicit in the blood of the saints, falls in a single hour under God's remembered judgment, mourned by the kings, merchants, and sailors who profited from her, even as heaven is summoned to rejoice, because her fall clears the way for the marriage of the Lamb.
section.frameNote: Six beats: an angel's cry that Babylon has fallen; a heavenly voice calling God's people to come out of her before her plagues arrive; the kings of the earth weeping at her smoke; the merchants mourning the loss of her luxury trade, cargo by cargo; the sailors lamenting from a distance; and heaven summoned to rejoice as a mighty angel casts her down like a great millstone, never to be found again.

units.label: The angel's cry: Babylon the great has fallen
units.note: a lair for demons and every unclean spirit

verses.text: After this I saw another angel descending from heaven with great authority, and the earth was illuminated by his glory.

And he cried out in a mighty voice: “{{epesen|Fallen, fallen}} is {{babylon|Babylon}} the great! She has become a lair for demons and a haunt for every unclean spirit, every unclean bird, and every detestable beast.

All the nations have drunk the wine of the passion of her immorality. The kings of the earth were immoral with her, and the {{emporos|merchants}} of the earth have grown wealthy from the extravagance of her {{strenos|luxury}}.”

units.label: Come out of her, My people
units.note: her sins piled up to heaven

verses.text: Then I heard another voice from heaven say: “{{exerchomai|Come out}} of her, My people, so that you will not share in her sins or contract any of her plagues.
For her sins are piled up to heaven, and God has remembered her iniquities.
Give back to her as she has done to others; pay her back double for what she has done; mix her a double portion in her own cup.
As much as she has glorified herself and lived in luxury, give her the same measure of torment and grief. In her heart she says, ‘I sit as queen; I am not a widow and will never see grief.’
Therefore her plagues will come in one day, death and grief and famine, and she will be consumed by fire, for mighty is the Lord God who judges her.”

units.label: The kings of the earth weep
units.note: in a single hour your judgment has come

verses.text: Then the kings of the earth who committed sexual immorality and lived in luxury with her will weep and wail at the sight of the smoke rising from the fire that consumes her.
In fear of her torment, they will stand at a distance and cry out: “Woe, woe to the great city, the mighty city of Babylon! For in a single hour your judgment has come.”

units.label: The merchants mourn her cargo
units.note: no one left to buy their goods

verses.text: And the merchants of the earth will weep and mourn over her, because there is no one left to buy their cargo:
cargo of gold, silver, precious stones, and pearls; of fine linen, purple, silk, and scarlet; of all kinds of citron wood and every article of ivory, precious wood, bronze, iron, and marble;
of cinnamon, spice, incense, myrrh, and frankincense; of wine, olive oil, fine flour, and wheat; of cattle, sheep, horses, and chariots; of slaves and souls of men.
And they will say: “The fruit of your soul's desire has departed from you; all your luxury and splendor have vanished, never to be seen again.”
The merchants who sold these things and grew their wealth from her will stand at a distance, in fear of her torment. They will weep and mourn,
saying: “Woe, woe to the great city, clothed in fine linen and purple and scarlet, adorned with gold and precious stones and pearls!

units.label: The sailors lament from a distance
units.note: what city was ever like this

verses.text: For in a single hour such fabulous wealth has been destroyed!” Every shipmaster, passenger, and sailor, and all who make their living from the sea, will stand at a distance
and cry out at the sight of the smoke rising from the fire that consumes her. “What city was ever like this great city?” they will exclaim.

Then they will throw dust on their heads as they weep and mourn and cry out: “Woe, woe to the great city, where all who had ships on the sea were enriched by her wealth! For in a single hour she has been destroyed.”

units.label: Heaven rejoices, and the millstone is cast down

verses.text: Rejoice over her, O heaven, O saints and apostles and prophets, because God has pronounced for you His judgment against her.
Then a mighty angel picked up a stone the size of a great millstone and cast it into the sea, saying: “With such violence the great city of Babylon will be cast down, never to be seen again.

And the sound of harpists and musicians, of flute players and trumpeters, will never ring out in you again. Nor will any craftsmen of any trade be found in you again, nor the sound of a millstone be heard in you again.

The light of a lamp will never shine in you again, and the voices of a bride and bridegroom will never call out in you again. For your merchants were the great ones of the earth, because all the nations were deceived by your sorcery.”
And there was found in her the blood of prophets and saints, and of all who had been slain on the earth.

epesen.gloss: Fell, has fallen, the aorist of pipto. John doubles the verb, epesen, epesen, for emphatic, dirge-like effect, directly echoing the taunt song over historical Babylon in Isaiah 21:9. The doubled cry announces Babylon's fall as already, prophetically, an accomplished fact, even before the narrative that follows unpacks it.

babylon.gloss: The Greek form of the ancient city's name. In Revelation it names not the literal Mesopotamian city, long fallen by John's day, but a symbolic Babylon, an idolatrous, luxury-drunk, blood-guilty world power, standing in Scripture's long tradition of Babylon as the archetype of humanity organized in defiance of God, from Genesis 11 onward.

emporos.gloss: A merchant or trader. The word and its cognates dominate the chapter's central section, cataloguing Babylon's vast trade in luxury goods and, devastatingly, slaves and souls of men. Their grief is not for Babylon's sin but for their own lost profit, exposing an economy built on exploitation as complicit in her judgment.

strenos.gloss: Luxury, sensuous excess, wanton self-indulgence. Related to the verb streniao, to live in reckless extravagance, the word appears repeatedly across the chapter to describe Babylon's manner of life; her judgment is measured out in exact proportion to it, the same measure of torment and grief she gave herself in luxury.

exerchomai.gloss: To come out, to go out. The heavenly voice's command, come out of her, My people, draws on the same verb used of Israel's exodus from Egypt and the later Old Testament call to flee Babylon, Jeremiah 51:45, Isaiah 48:20, casting Babylon's judgment as a fresh occasion for God's people to separate themselves from complicity in her sins.

basic.context: An angel announces that Babylon the great has fallen, and a voice from heaven calls God's people to come out of her before her sudden judgment arrives. What follows is a threefold dirge: the kings, the merchants, and the sailors of the world all watch her smoke from a distance and mourn, each grieving the loss of what she gave them, wealth, luxury, and profit, rather than grieving her sin. The chapter ends with heaven summoned to rejoice, and a mighty angel casts a great millstone into the sea to picture Babylon's sudden, final, irreversible fall.
basic.hermeneutics: Christians disagree on whether this fall points mainly to a past historical judgment, most obviously the collapse of pagan Rome, or to a still-future or ongoing pattern of judgment on every Babylon-like system of idolatrous wealth and power throughout history. The debate matters less than the chapter's clear moral center: whatever wears Babylon's character, an economy and culture built on exploitation, idolatry, and violence against God's people, will be judged suddenly and completely, and God's people are called to come out of it now.
basic.originalLanguages: The angel's cry doubles the Greek verb epesen, fallen, fallen, turning Babylon's judgment into an Old Testament-style taunt song. Her name, Babylon, gathers up Scripture's whole story of organized human defiance of God since Genesis 11. Her strenos, her reckless luxury, becomes the very measure of her judgment, and the emporoi, the merchants, mourn their lost trade more than her sin. And the call to exerchomai, come out, echoes Israel's ancient exodus from Egypt and the prophets' call to flee historical Babylon.
basic.typology: Babylon's sudden, complete fall, pictured as a great millstone cast into the sea, never to be found again, fulfills and intensifies Jeremiah's own symbolic act of sinking a scroll of judgment against historical Babylon in the Euphrates, showing the certainty and finality of divine judgment on organized evil.
basic.christ: The chapter's dirges over lost wealth stand in sharp, deliberate contrast to the wedding announced in the next chapter; Babylon's fall clears the world's stage for the marriage of the Lamb, showing that Christ's joy, not the world's luxury, is the true and lasting treasure.
basic.god: God is shown as the Judge who remembers sins piled up to heaven and repays exactly, in the same measure given, yet He is also the God who warns His people beforehand, come out of her, My people, so that judgment on Babylon is never meant to catch His own off guard.
basic.crossReferences: Isaiah 21 and Jeremiah 50-51 supply the taunt song and the command to flee historical Babylon that this chapter echoes. Ezekiel 27 supplies the cargo-list lament over Tyre that shapes the merchants' dirge here. And Revelation 19 supplies the wedding of the Lamb that immediately answers Babylon's fall with joy.
basic.oneStory: From Babel's tower to Babylon's exile to Rome's empire, Scripture tells one story of human civilization organizing itself in luxury, idolatry, and violence against God's people, and always, eventually, falling. This chapter's dirge is Scripture's last word on that pattern: come out of her now, because her fall is certain, sudden, and final, and it clears the way for the marriage of the Lamb.

context.literary:
Revelation 18 is built as a funeral service for a city that has not yet been told it is dead. The chapter has five movements. An angel of great glory proclaims the fall, verses 1 to 3. A second voice from heaven turns from announcement to command, verses 4 to 8, with imperatives aimed at God's people and at the executioners alike. Three groups of mourners then take the stage in turn: the kings, verses 9 and 10, the merchants, verses 11 to 17a, and the seafarers, verses 17b to 19. Heaven answers them with a summons to rejoice, verse 20. Finally a strong angel acts out the sentence with a stone, and a last accusation is read over the ruins, verses 21 to 24.

Notice how the three laments rhyme. Each group stands 'at a distance' for fear of her torment, each cries 'Woe, woe to the great city,' and each ends on the same phrase, 'in a single hour,' verses 10, 17 and 19. The refrain turns the slow, grinding story of an empire into one stroke of the clock. The structure also moves downward through the social ladder, from rulers to traders to the working crews, and the middle lament is by far the longest. John gives the cargo list more space than the kings or the sailors, because the city's real religion is revealed in what she bought.

Four times in verses 21 to 23 the chapter says 'never again' or 'no more', and each line takes away one ordinary sound of city life: music, craft, grinding grain, lamplight, wedding voices. The effect is a city fading into silence. Chapter 18 also mirrors the chapter before it. In chapter 17 John sees the prostitute and is given an interpretation; in chapter 18 he hears what her fall means for everyone who lived off her.
context.historical:
The cargo list in verses 12 and 13 is a catalogue of Mediterranean luxury, and it ends with the line that would have hurt first century hearers most: 'slaves and souls of men.' Rome's wealth flowed in by sea from the whole known world. Grain ships from Egypt fed the capital, and the harbour at Puteoli and later Ostia was thick with traders. Shipmasters, passengers and sailors in verse 17 are the people who made that machine run. The Roman peace, the pax Romana, gave merchants safe roads and sea lanes, and Asia Minor, where these seven churches lived, grew rich on it.

The list also echoes the oracle against Tyre in Ezekiel 27, where the seaport's trade partners and goods are itemised, and Ezekiel 27:13 itself names slaves among the merchandise. John has taken the Old Testament's portrait of a trading empire and fitted it over his own day. The line about 'sorcery' in verse 23 has the same borrowed texture, since Nahum 3:4 accuses Nineveh of the same thing.

For believers the economic pressure was personal. Trade guilds met under the patronage of local gods and the emperor, and meals at their feasts involved offering to those gods, as the letters to Pergamum and Thyatira already hinted, Revelation 2:14 and 2:20. To refuse the idols could mean losing the means to buy or sell. This is why the call to 'come out of her' in verse 4 is not abstract. It names a cost: leave the circuit of profit that depends on the city's gods and you may be poorer. That is also why the merchants' grief is so pointed. They weep because the market closed.

Finally, Babylon the empire had a long afterlife as a name. By John's day the great Euphrates city was a faded ruin, and Jewish writers after AD 70 used Babylon as a code for Rome, which had also destroyed a temple in Jerusalem. John's first readers would hear the name as a code they already knew.
context.canonical:
Chapter 18 is a mosaic of earlier Scripture, and almost every verse has an Old Testament source. The opening cry, 'Fallen, fallen is Babylon,' comes from Isaiah 21:9 and was already quoted in Revelation 14:8. The call to flee reaches back to Jeremiah 51:6 and 51:45, the desolation to Isaiah 13:21 and 34:11 (the haunts of wild creatures in ruins), the boast of verse 7 to Isaiah 47:8, 'I am, and there is none besides me,' and the stone sunk in the sea to Jeremiah 51:63 and 51:64, where a scroll of judgment is tied to a stone and thrown into the Euphrates. The silencing of bridal voices and millstones in verse 22 and 23 is straight from Jeremiah 25:10. John is reading Israel's prophets as one unified verdict against every power that sets itself up as God.

The story begins long before the prophets. Babylon's ancestor is the city on the plain of Shinar, where people said, 'let us build for ourselves a city with a tower that reaches to the heavens,' Genesis 11:4. From that first tower to Nebuchadnezzar to Rome, 'Babylon' becomes the Bible's name for human pride organised as civilisation. Its opposite appears at the very next scene, the bride and the holy city of chapters 19 to 21.

Within Revelation the chapter belongs to a pair with the New Jerusalem. Both are called a city, both are described as a woman, and both are clothed and adorned. One is the harlot; the other the bride. The 'blood of prophets and saints' that closes the chapter in verse 24 balances the martyrs' cry in Revelation 6:10, 'How long, O Lord,' and the angel's verdict that they have been answered. Jesus had already pointed to this long ledger when He told the leaders of His day that the blood of all the prophets would be charged to that generation, Luke 11:50, so the New Testament links the verdict to more than one city.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
John wrote to churches that were being tempted not only by persecution but by comfort. The Lord's complaint against Laodicea, 'I am rich, and have acquired wealth, and have need of nothing,' Revelation 3:17, shows the danger was a well fed spirit. This chapter is meant to break that spell by letting the reader hear the sound of the city's end. When Babylon's fall is described from the viewpoint of those who profited from her, the reader sees how thin the 'security' was. Every voice that mourns is a self interested one. Nobody in the chapter weeps for justice lost.

John also means to give his readers a verb to obey. The command 'Come out of her, My people' stands between the announcement of the fall and its details, so that the doom is not just information but an invitation, as the prophets' warnings always were. The point is to bring people out before the hour comes. For the martyrs, he wanted them to hear the grievance recorded in verse 24 as seen and counted, so that their patient endurance could rest on God's justice rather than on revenge.

He did not mean them to read the dirge as a political plan. There is no call to take up arms, withhold taxes or storm the city. The church's only action is to withdraw its heart and its complicity, and to rejoice in heaven's verdict when it comes.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter describes a city, her buyers and her fall. What it commands is short: come out, verse 4, and rejoice, verse 20. The grim instructions in verse 6, to pay her back double, are addressed to the executioners of judgment, not to the church, and nothing in the New Testament turns them into a rule for believers, who are told never to repay evil for evil, Romans 12:17 to 19. The scene is a ruling already made by God, not a licence for revenge.

Applying it today requires care. The text does not hand us a list of businesses or governments to boycott. It gives us tests: does a system trade in human beings, treat luxury as a god, feed on violence against God's people, and deceive the nations with its glamour? Where such marks appear, the call to come out applies, and it can include ordinary decisions, what we profit from, what we buy, whom we flatter. Yet the chapter also stops short of calling believers to leave every city or trade. Daniel served in Babylon and Jeremiah told exiles to seek its welfare, Jeremiah 29:7. The line runs through the heart, not the map.

debates.question: Who or what is Babylon?

views.label: Rome, the first century empire
views.case: John explicitly describes a city on seven hills in Revelation 17:9, ruling over the kings of the earth, 17:18, and Jewish and Christian writers of his time used Babylon as a code name for Rome. The trade, the luxury, the imperial cult and the persecution of Christians all match. First hearers would not have needed a decoder.

views.label: The world system in every age
views.case: Others stress that John gives no proper address and pieces her portrait from Babylon, Tyre and Nineveh, three different cities, so that she becomes a type of every power that unites commerce, religion and violence. Rome was her first costume, not her only one. This view notes that Revelation also calls the great city 'Sodom and Egypt' in 11:8, plainly symbolic names.

views.label: A future city, a rebuilt Babylon or a coming world capital
views.case: A further reading holds that the prophecy awaits a literal city, sometimes pictured as a rebuilt Babylon on the Euphrates or a final global capital, because Isaiah's and Jeremiah's oracles against Babylon were not fulfilled in every detail by the ancient fall. Supporters point to Revelation 16:19 and 17:5.

debates.bearing: All three readings hold that the city is under judgment and that what she stands for is an idolatrous alliance of money and power. The disagreement is about the address, not about the verdict or about what God's people should do. A reader may hold the identification loosely and still obey 'Come out of her.'

debates.question: To whom is the command 'Give back to her as she has done' addressed?

views.label: To the angels or heavenly agents who carry out judgment
views.case: The plural imperatives of verse 6 come from a voice from heaven, and judgment in Revelation is regularly carried out by angels and heavenly forces, as with the bowls in chapter 16. The speaker is the same voice that calls God's people, and the executioners are left unspecified.

views.label: To God's people, as a call to prayer or witness
views.case: Because the voice speaks immediately after 'My people,' some hear verse 6 as addressed to the same audience, so that the saints' prayers, as in Revelation 6:10, take part in the judgment. On this view believers do not strike, but they echo the cry of the martyrs and ask for justice.

views.label: To the kings and nations who turn on her
views.case: A third option notes that in Revelation 17:16 the ten kings hate the prostitute and burn her, so God uses her own allies as His instrument, and verse 6 may be heard in that light.

debates.bearing: The text leaves the audience unnamed on purpose, and what is plain is the principle: payment in kind. The measure she gave to others comes back. Whoever carries it out, Revelation never gives the church a sword here, and Romans 12:19 tells believers to leave room for God's wrath.

study.originalLanguages:
The first thing to notice in verse 2 is that Babylon becomes a 'lair,' katoiketerion, and a 'haunt,' phylake, for demons, unclean spirits and unclean birds. Katoiketerion is the word Paul uses for the church as 'a dwelling place for God in the Spirit,' Ephesians 2:22. The city that should have been a home for the divine presence became a home for the opposite. Phylake is a watch post or a prison, and the same word appears again in Revelation 20:7, where Satan is released 'from his prison.' So the demon haunted ruin and the dragon's cell are in the same family of words.

The 'wine of the passion of her immorality' in verse 3 joins porneia, sexual and spiritual unfaithfulness, with thymos, which can mean 'passion' or 'wrath.' Revelation 14:8 uses the same phrase, and 14:10 speaks of the 'wine of God's wrath,' with the same noun. The nations drink her passion and so, in the end, drink God's wrath. The ambiguity is probably the point, since the cup of desire becomes the cup of judgment.

In verse 5 her sins are 'piled up to heaven.' The verb behind it, ekollethesan, is a form of kollao, to stick or join together, as if her sins had been glued into a tower reaching the sky. The picture quietly recalls the tower of Genesis 11:4. God 'remembered' her iniquities, the same verb of divine remembrance used for Babylon in Revelation 16:19, and it is the vocabulary of covenant mercy turned to judgment.

The command in verse 6 to give her 'double' draws on a Hebrew way of speaking where 'double' means full, equivalent measure, as in Isaiah 40:2 and Jeremiah 16:18. The next line says 'the same measure of torment,' so the judgment matches the offence rather than exceeding it. The Greek for torment, basanismos, appears in verses 7, 10 and 15 and returns in Revelation 14:11, where it is linked to the smoke that rises, which is exactly the smoke Babylon's mourners watch in verse 9.

Verse 7 has her claim, 'I sit as queen,' with the present tense of 'sit,' kathemai, a posture of permanence. The claim 'I am not a widow' is lifted from Isaiah 47:8, where the same Babylon said 'I will never be a widow.' The verse is an echo that deliberately repeats a prophetic taunt.

In verse 13 the final cargo items read, literally, 'bodies and souls of men.' The Greek word for bodies, somata, was the ordinary slave market term. 'And souls' is added, so that the last two words of the cargo list protest that these are not merchandise but people. Verse 23 adds that the nations were deceived by her 'sorcery,' pharmakeia, a word that also appears in Galatians 5:20 in a list of works of the flesh. It covers drug, potion and spell, and it points to the intoxication of prosperity that holds the nations spellbound.

typology.type: The great millstone cast into the sea, Revelation 18:21
typology.fulfillment: The sign-act repeats Jeremiah's action in Jeremiah 51:63 and 51:64, where a scroll weighted with a stone sinks in the Euphrates as a picture of Babylon's end. The correspondence is exact: a heavy object, deep water, and 'never again.' In Revelation the act is performed by an angel on the entire city, and the mourners confirm it by dust on their heads. Jesus used the same image of a millstone around the neck for anyone who leads little ones astray, Matthew 18:6, so this closing sign binds Babylon's fall to the way she deceived and destroyed the weak. The type falls short because Jeremiah's stone sank one ancient city; John's stone speaks of the end of Babylon in every age.

Lot was pulled from Sodom, Genesis 19:15 to 17, Israel left Egypt at the first passover, and exiles were told to flee Babylon in Jeremiah 51:6 and 51:45. Each time God's people were called out before the blow fell. The pattern reaches its fullest form in Christ, who died outside the city gate 'to sanctify the people by His own blood,' Hebrews 13:12, and who invites believers to 'go to Him outside the camp,' Hebrews 13:13. The new exodus is not a march from a place but a movement toward Him. It falls short of the type in one way: Lot fled a single city by a single road, while believers today are called out of a system that spans the world.

typology.type: Babylon the harlot city and the bride city
typology.fulfillment: The Old Testament prophets already spoke of Jerusalem as a faithful city turned prostitute, Isaiah 1:21, and of Israel as a bride, Hosea 2:19 and 2:20. Revelation draws two cities as two women. Babylon is arrayed 'in fine linen and purple and scarlet' and she boasts as queen, Revelation 18:16, 18:7. The bride is also clothed in fine linen, but in the next chapter it is explicitly given to her, Revelation 19:8. The correspondence is the same woman-city image, and the escalation is that the end of one city opens into the wedding of the other. The type is limited in that Babylon is never rebuilt or reformed; the harlot is judged, the bride is renewed.

typology.type: Fallen empires as signs of the final fall
typology.fulfillment: Tyre, Nineveh and the Babylon of Nebuchadnezzar each fell in the Old Testament and each oracle was seen as God's verdict on an arrogant trading power, as in Ezekiel 27 and Nahum 3. John gathers these into one dirge, so that each fallen empire stands as an early installment of the last. Christ gives the pattern its meaning, since all earthly kingdoms are measured by the stone cut out without hands that fills the earth, Daniel 2:34 and 2:35, and by His own claim, 'My kingdom is not of this world,' John 18:36. The pattern is partial because those earlier fallings did not end the world's longing for such empires; only the return of the King does.

study.christ:
Christ is not named in Revelation 18, and that silence is worth noticing. The whole chapter is a chapter about what Babylon says and what her friends say. The heaven that rejoices at her fall in verse 20 does so only because 'God has pronounced for you His judgment against her,' which is the Lamb's own vindication of His witnesses. The links to Christ lie in what the chapter takes away and in what He had already said.

The first link is the contrast of kingdoms. The merchants sell 'slaves and souls of men,' verse 13. Jesus describes His own mission in the opposite terms: 'the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give His life as a ransom for many,' Mark 10:45. The city buys and sells bodies; the Lamb buys people 'for God' with His blood, Revelation 5:9. Where Babylon trades in persons, Christ redeems them.

A second link is the voice that says 'Come out of her, My people.' The speaker is not named but belongs to heaven, and the possessive 'My people' is the Lord's own language for the flock. Jesus said that His sheep hear His voice and follow Him, John 10:27, and He called His disciples out of the world's grip while leaving them in the world, John 17:15 and 17:16. The cry of Revelation 18:4 is the shepherd's voice in the language of the prophets.

A third link is Jesus' teaching about wealth. 'You cannot serve both God and money,' Matthew 6:24, and the rich fool's night, Luke 12:20, are what the dirge dramatises. The merchants' final line, 'in a single hour such fabulous wealth has been destroyed,' is the word of the Lord's parable played out on a world stage.

Fourth, the chapter closes with 'the blood of prophets and saints' found in her. Jesus said that the blood of all the prophets, 'from the foundation of the world,' would be charged against that generation, Luke 11:50 and 11:51. The Lamb is the one who keeps the ledger and the one who was himself slain. The same blood that Babylon spilled is answered by the blood that redeems. Because Christ rose, the martyrs' death is not the last word, and Babylon's apparent triumph is shown to be a thin shell.

The reading should be held honestly. Revelation 18 does not allegorise the millstone as the cross or the merchants as the Pharisees. Its link to Christ rests on New Testament teaching about the Lamb, His people, His redemption and His judgment, and on the chapter's place just before the marriage supper. Christ's name appears next, when heaven shouts and the wedding is announced.
study.god:
The first thing the chapter shows about God is that He keeps a record. The sins are 'piled up to heaven' and 'God has remembered her iniquities,' verse 5. This is not forgetfulness, nor an angry reflex. It is the patient memory of a judge who counts blood, as when He said to Cain, 'Your brother's blood cries out to Me from the ground,' Genesis 4:10. In verse 24 He finds in her 'the blood of prophets and saints, and of all who had been slain on the earth,' so that one city is held responsible for every victim of her pattern. God does not lose a single name.

He is also just in the strict sense of fit. The sentence in verses 6 and 7 matches the crime, 'the same measure,' and the sentence speaks to her boast: she said 'I sit as queen' and receives grief. Judgment mirrors sin. It does not exceed what she did and it is not arbitrary. 'Mighty is the Lord God who judges her,' verse 8, makes the point that this is an act of strength, not of rage, which fits the words of Deuteronomy 32:4, 'His works are perfect, and all His ways are just.'

God is the one who calls His own to safety. The command 'Come out of her, My people' shows a God who warns before He strikes, as He warned Noah, Lot and Israel in Egypt. The call is a mercy, and the words 'My people' tell us that He claims them even while they stand in the middle of Babylon. The Lord does not rescue by removing believers from history, but by calling them to refuse what the city worships.

He rules economies and cities, not only individual hearts. The list of trade goods is a reminder that nothing in the market lies outside His judgement. Gold, silk, spices, grain and bodies pass under His eyes, and the lament that follows shows that God cares about how wealth is made. The God of Revelation is the one who also created and owns 'the earth and everything in it,' Psalm 24:1, so luxury built on exploitation is theft from Him.

Finally, He is sovereign over the timing. 'In a single hour' declares that the great powers of earth are brief. The kings, the merchants and the sailors cannot hold the city back. The God who sits on the throne in Revelation 4 and 5 does not need an army to dispatch an empire, and He does not hurry.

For worship, the chapter teaches us to let God's verdicts be true and to rejoice when they come, as heaven does in verse 20, without gloating over the people involved. It also warns us that sorrow for lost comfort is not repentance. The merchants lament and never repent. A worshiper learns to mourn the sin, not the loss of a market, and to hold wealth with open hands.

crossReferences.note: The source of the opening cry. Isaiah heard riders announce that Babylon had fallen and that the images of her gods lay shattered on the ground. John takes the double cry and makes it a verdict that stands over every later Babylon, with the idols of her wealth as the ones that fail.

The source of the call to leave. Jeremiah told exiles to come out of Babylon and save their lives from the fierce anger of the LORD. Revelation 18:4 gives the very same command to the church, turning a historical flight from a city into a continuing summons to separate from her sins.

Babylon's boast in verse 7 is lifted from here, where she says she will never be a widow or know the loss of children. John shows that the same pride repeats in every age, and that the sentence which fell on the old city, loss arriving in a moment, falls on the new one.

Tyre's merchants, and the list of goods they handled, including slaves, stand behind the cargo list of Revelation 18:12 and 18:13. Ezekiel mourned a city destroyed by the sea; John adds one pitiless detail, that the trade included human souls, and extends the lament to the whole world's economy.

Jeremiah tied a stone to a scroll and threw it into the Euphrates as a sign that Babylon would sink and not rise again. The mighty angel's millstone in Revelation 18:21 is the same act on a larger scale, and the phrase 'never to be seen again' echoes 'never rise again.'

The silencing of joy and gladness, the voices of the bride and bridegroom, the sound of millstones and the light of the lamp, is Jeremiah's description of Judah's own ruin. John uses it for Babylon in verses 22 and 23, so the same loss that Israel suffered for faithlessness comes upon the empire that corrupted the world.

The first Babylon is the city with the tower that reaches the heavens, built so that people could make a name for themselves. Revelation 18:5 says her sins are piled up to heaven, a wry reversal. Human attempts to reach heaven only pile up guilt, and God answers from above.

The martyrs under the altar cry 'How long, O Lord, until You avenge our blood?' Chapter 18 is the answer. Verse 20 invites the saints to rejoice because God has judged for them, and verse 24 records the blood found in her. The delay was patience, not neglect.

Jesus says no one can serve two masters and names money as the rival to God. The merchants of Revelation 18 are people who chose the other master and now lose everything with it. The chapter is the large scale picture of what the Sermon on the Mount warns against in the single heart.

Believers are told to go out to Jesus outside the camp, bearing His disgrace. It gives the positive side of 'Come out of her.' The exit from Babylon is also an entrance, to the Lord who suffered outside the gate, and it carries the same cost of reproach.

Paul tells believers not to take revenge but to leave room for God's wrath, because vengeance belongs to Him. The commands of Revelation 18:6 fit this: the one who pays Babylon back is God, and heaven's rejoicing in verse 20 is the church's response to a verdict it did not execute.

John warns against loving the world and notes that the world and its desires pass away, while the one who does God's will remains forever. The chapter shows this principle at the scale of a city: all the splendour vanishes in an hour, and the only thing that remains is what is done for God.

study.oneStory:
The story of Scripture begins with a garden and a command, and the first human city, Cain's in Genesis 4:17, is built east of Eden by a murderer's line. Babylon grows from that root. Genesis 11 gives its first form, a city and a tower set against dispersal, and the Old Testament then watches one power after another carry the same spirit: Egypt, Assyria, Tyre, and the Babylon that burned the temple. Chapter 18 gathers these into a single figure so that the long story of human self rule can be seen to its end.

Within the book, Babylon is the harlot of chapter 17, the great city of 16:19, and the counter-city of the bride. The earlier question of the seals, 'How long?', is met here. The dragon, the beast and the false prophet make war on the Lamb, and chapter 18 shows the economic and cultural wing of their alliance being dismantled. What chapter 17 said in symbol, that the beast hates the harlot and turns on her, chapter 18 says in lament.

The chapter also sets up the next scene. The silence of 'the voices of a bride and bridegroom' in verse 23 is answered at once in Revelation 19:7, where a different bride is ready. The sound of 'harpists and musicians' that will never ring out in Babylon returns as the roar of a great multitude shouting 'Hallelujah' in heaven. The stone cast in the sea leads directly into the marriage supper, and the story moves from funeral to feast with no gap.

The end of the story is the New Jerusalem. The city that Abraham looked for, 'whose architect and builder is God,' Hebrews 11:10, comes down from heaven in Revelation 21:2, and its gates are never shut, nothing unclean enters, and 'the kings of the earth will bring their glory into it,' Revelation 21:24 and 21:27. Babylon's wealth was gathered by exploitation and ended in smoke. The new city's wealth is the glory of the nations, redeemed and brought in. In the new creation, trade, craft, music, lamplight and wedding voices all return, as the very things Babylon's fall removed, and they return as gifts under the Lamb's light, Revelation 21:23.

sermon.title: Revelation (Part 20): Revelation 17-18
sermon.why: Carson's sermon directly covers Revelation 18, describing it as a dirge or lament over Babylon's fall in which she receives exactly what she deserves, matching this study's passage and theme precisely.

quiz.q: Why do the kings, merchants, and sailors mourn Babylon's fall?

options.text: They grieve the loss of the wealth, luxury, and profit she gave them, not her sin against God.
options.note: Revelation 18:9-19 shows their grief is entirely for lost wealth and trade.

options.text: They grieve because they loved her righteousness and feared losing a godly example.
options.note: Babylon is condemned as sinful and blood-guilty, not righteous.

options.text: They mourn because they expect to be judged alongside her.
options.note: Their laments focus on lost profit and luxury, not fear of their own judgment.

options.text: They do not mourn at all; the chapter describes only celebration.
options.note: The chapter describes extensive weeping and wailing from the kings, merchants, and sailors.

quiz.q: What does the heavenly voice command God's people to do in verse 4?

options.text: Come out of her, so that they do not share in her sins or receive her plagues.
options.note: Revelation 18:4 gives this command directly.

options.text: Stay in Babylon to witness to her merchants.
options.note: The command is to come out, not remain.

options.text: Join her feast to demonstrate Christian freedom.
options.note: The command is separation from her sins, not participation.

options.text: Wait for the angel's permission before making any response.
options.note: The command is immediate and direct, not conditional on further permission.

quiz.q: How is Babylon's judgment measured out, according to verse 7?

options.text: In the same measure she glorified herself and lived in luxury, that same measure of torment and grief is given back to her.
options.note: Revelation 18:7 states this exact principle of proportional judgment.

options.text: Far less severely than her actual sins deserved.
options.note: The text describes exact, proportional repayment, not leniency.

options.text: Randomly, without any relation to what she had done.
options.note: The judgment is explicitly measured against her own self-glorification and luxury.

options.text: She receives no judgment at all in this chapter.
options.note: The whole chapter describes her sudden and severe judgment.

quiz.q: What does the mighty angel's millstone, thrown into the sea, picture?

options.text: The sudden, violent, and irreversible fall of Babylon, never to be found again.
options.note: Revelation 18:21 gives this exact interpretation of the enacted sign.

options.text: A blessing given to Babylon's faithful remnant.
options.note: The millstone pictures destruction, not blessing.

options.text: The rebuilding of Babylon after a period of judgment.
options.note: The text insists she will never be found again, ruling out rebuilding.

options.text: A literal execution method used against her merchants.
options.note: The millstone is a symbolic sign-act picturing the city's fall, not a literal execution.

quiz.q: What is found in Babylon at the chapter's close, verse 24?

options.text: The blood of prophets and saints, and of all who had been slain on the earth.
options.note: Revelation 18:24 states this as the final indictment against her.

options.text: A remnant of righteous worshipers spared from judgment.
options.note: The verse describes the guilt found in her, not a spared remnant.

options.text: Treasures later restored to the nations.
options.note: The chapter describes total loss of her wealth, not restoration.

options.text: Nothing; the city is described as entirely empty of any remains.
options.note: The text specifically names what was found in her, the blood of the slain.

questions: The kings, merchants, and sailors weep for what Babylon gave them, not for her sin. Where might you find yourself more attached to what a corrupt system provides you than concerned about the harm it causes others?

Come out of her, My people is a call to active separation, not passive distance. What would it look like this week to actually step back from something that quietly makes you complicit in exploitation or idolatry?
Babylon's merchants trade in everything, down to slaves and souls of men. Where do you see people treated as commodities today, and how might you respond differently than the world's economy does?

Heaven is summoned to rejoice at Babylon's fall, because God has pronounced judgment for His saints, not merely against Babylon. How does it change your view of God's judgment to know it vindicates His suffering people?

This whole dark chapter exists to clear the stage for the wedding of the Lamb in chapter 19. When you feel weighed down by the world's corruption, how does looking ahead to that wedding feast give you hope?

translationNotes.note: Fallen, fallen translates a doubled Greek verb, epesen epesen, a deliberate Hebraic dirge form quoting Isaiah 21:9 almost word for word; some translations render it as a single has fallen, but the doubling intensifies the finality of the announcement.
Luxury and related phrases translate strenos and its cognate verb, sometimes rendered sensuality or wantonness in other versions, capturing not mere comfort but reckless, self-indulgent excess.

The cargo list is deliberately exhaustive, moving from precious metals and stones through fabrics, foods, and livestock to, devastatingly, slaves and souls of men at the very end, a translation choice, some versions render simply bodies, that makes plain the list's final horror, human trafficking.

Come out of her uses the same Greek verb, exerchomai, found in the Greek Old Testament's call for Israel to leave Egypt and Babylon; translators consistently preserve this exodus echo across versions.

meta.notes: BSB text supplied pre-verified this session. The angel's cry in verses 2-3 is rendered as one continuous quotation, since the source text's quotation marks span both verses as a single utterance. Poetic line breaks, where present in the source, were flattened into flowing prose per this repo's convention.
